findings.source_quote: οἰκείων, γυναικὸς ἢ τέκνων ἢ ἀδελ-. φῶν ἢ γονέων ἢ φίλων ἢ ἄλλων τινῶν
findings.english_quote: We are also susceptible to grief, so that we may have sympathy at the death of members of our household—a wife, children, brothers, parents, friends, or anyone else.
findings.issue: “Members of our household” imposes a domestic-membership restriction on the entire following list. Here οἰκείων can designate people close to someone, and the explicit inclusion of friends and other people supports that broader relational sense rather than household membership.
findings.suggested_revision: Replace the relevant wording with “at the death of those close to us—a wife, children, brothers, parents, friends, or others.” Submit the revised sentence for fresh review.

findings.source_quote: καὶ πρὸς τὸ μὴ πάσχειν καὶ ἄλλους αὐτὸν θεραπεῦσαι δυνάμενος εὕρῃς.
findings.english_quote: and besides not suffering, you will find him able to heal others as well.
findings.issue: The supplied reading has nominative δυνάμενος, whereas the English predicates the ability of the person represented by accusative αὐτὸν. The ensuing example of Moses healing others supports this contextual interpretation of the irregular construction, so the rendering need not be blocked. Nevertheless, the case mismatch and the material alternative attachment to the addressed person are not disclosed anywhere in the draft notes.
findings.suggested_revision: Add a note quoting the supplied construction exactly. Explain that the main rendering understands the healing ability as belonging to the sinless person despite the printed nominative, with the following Moses example supporting that choice. Preserve the alternative nominative attachment to the addressee: approximately, “you, being able to heal others as well, may find him.” Do not silently replace δυνάμενος with δυνάμενον or characterize the verified print as an OCR error. The revised text and notes require fresh review.

findings.source_quote: τὸ γὰρ νενικῆσθαί σε ἔργῳ εἴδομεν, τὸν δὲ ἐπαγγελλόμενόν σου λόγον ἠκούσαμεν.
findings.english_quote: For we have seen your defeat in action and have heard your promised argument.
findings.issue: “Have heard your promised argument” naturally suggests that the substantive argument Simon promised has already been heard. That does not clearly represent the contrast between defeat demonstrated in action and promise-making speech merely heard. The draft's note expressly says the argument has not already been delivered, but the main wording fails to communicate that distinction. The following prediction that Simon will not return further supports rendering the heard λόγος as words of promise.
findings.suggested_revision: Use a source-transparent rendering such as “For we have seen your defeat in action, but have heard your words of promise.” Revise the lexical note to explain the promise-making sense of ἐπαγγελλόμενον in this contrast, while retaining any defensible alternative interpretation. This replacement remains a proposal requiring fresh review.
